STEP 1 — PRE-COMMITMENT  
Causal identification strategy: A two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (DiD) design that exploits (i) birth-cohort exposure to INPRES (young cohorts 1968-72 fully exposed vs. older cohorts 1950-62 not exposed) and (ii) cross-district variation in program intensity (number of INPRES schools built per 1,000 children in the district). The causal parameter of interest is the coefficient β on the interaction TreatmentCohortᵢ × ProgramIntensity_d.  
Directional hypothesis H₁: β > 0 — greater program intensity (more schools built) raises (a) individual years of schooling and (b) log real wages in adulthood.

STEP 2 — SPECIFICATION DISCIPLINE  
Exactly five linear regression specifications are pre-committed. All regressions cluster standard errors at the district level.

1. Schooling Baseline  
Yi = α + β (TreatmentCohortᵢ × ProgramIntensity_d) + δ_d + γ_c + εᵢ

 Yi: years of schooling  
 δ_d: district of birth fixed effects  
 γ_c: birth-year fixed effects  

2. Schooling + Individual Controls  
Add controls for age at survey, age², and an indicator for urban birth.

3. Schooling + Pre-trend Check  
Same as (1) but sample restricted to PRE-program cohorts (1950-62). Replace TreatmentCohort with a pseudo-treatment indicator for cohorts 1960-62 (should be zero effect).

4. Wages Baseline  
log(Wageᵢ) = α + β (TreatmentCohortᵢ × ProgramIntensity_d) + δ_d + γ_c + εᵢ  
Sample: wage earners only.

5. Wages + Schooling Control  
Same as (4) but add individual schooling as a control to test whether earnings effects operate through education.

No further specifications will be estimated.

STEP 3 — FALSIFICATION GATE  
The directional hypothesis is rejected if ANY of the following occur:  
• In Spec 1 the estimated β ≤ 0 or its two-sided p-value > 0.10.  
• In Spec 3 the estimated β is statistically different from zero at the 10 % level (|t| > 1.64), indicating a violated pre-trend.  
• For wages, if Spec 4 yields β ≤ 0 or p > 0.10.  
(All other results are secondary; the gate hinges on Specs 1, 3, 4.)

STEP 4 — R CODE (self-contained)

```r
#----- Load packages -----
library(data.table)            # Efficient data handling
library(fixest)                # For fast fixed-effects regressions

#----- Read data -----
supas   <- fread("supas_1995_individual.csv")      # individual survey
program <- fread("inpres_schools_7378.csv")        # district INPRES counts
enroll  <- fread("enrollment_1971.csv")            # not used in specs but could merge

#----- Construct key variables -----
# Merge program intensity to individuals by district of birth
supas <- merge(supas, program, by = "district_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Program intensity: schools per 1,000 primary-age children (variable already computed)
# Treatment cohort indicator
supas[, treat_cohort := birth_year %between% c(1968, 1972)]

# Specifications run on full sample unless otherwise stated
# Clustered standard errors at district level with fixest (cluster = "id")
cluster_var <- "district_id"

#----- SPEC 1: Schooling Baseline -----
spec1 <- feols(school_years ~ treat_cohort*program_intensity | district_id + birth_year,
               data = supas, cluster = cluster_var)

#----- SPEC 2: Schooling + Controls -----
spec2 <- feols(school_years ~ treat_cohort*program_intensity + age + I(age^2) + urban_birth |
                 district_id + birth_year,
               data = supas, cluster = cluster_var)

#----- SPEC 3: Pre-trend (older cohorts only) -----
pre_sample <- supas[birth_year %between% c(1950, 1962)]
pre_sample[, pseudo_treat := birth_year %between% c(1960, 1962)]
spec3 <- feols(school_years ~ pseudo_treat*program_intensity | district_id + birth_year,
               data = pre_sample, cluster = cluster_var)

#----- SPEC 4: Wages Baseline -----
wage_sample <- supas[!is.na(real_wage)]        # restrict to wage earners
spec4 <- feols(log(real_wage) ~ treat_cohort*program_intensity | district_id + birth_year,
               data = wage_sample, cluster = cluster_var)

#----- SPEC 5: Wages + Schooling Control -----
spec5 <- feols(log(real_wage) ~ treat_cohort*program_intensity + school_years |
                 district_id + birth_year,
               data = wage_sample, cluster = cluster_var)

#----- Display results -----
etable(list(spec1, spec2, spec3, spec4, spec5),
       keep = "treat_cohort:program_intensity|pseudo_treat:program_intensity")
```

STEP 5 — FINDINGS & GATE ASSESSMENT (expected)  
Based on prior literature, I expect:

• Spec 1: β̂ ≈ 0.12 (s.e. ≈ 0.04) ⇒ p ≈ 0.003  
• Spec 2: β̂ drops to ≈ 0.11 (s.e. ≈ 0.04)  
• Spec 3: β̂ ≈ 0.01 (s.e. ≈ 0.03) ⇒ not statistically different from zero (pre-trend satisfied)  
• Spec 4: β̂ ≈ 0.08 log-points (s.e. ≈ 0.04) ⇒ p ≈ 0.05  
• Spec 5: β̂ falls to ≈ 0.03 (s.e. ≈ 0.03), suggesting education mediates earnings.

Gate assessment: All three gate criteria are expected to be met (positive and significant β in Specs 1 & 4; null effect in Spec 3). Therefore the falsification gate would NOT be triggered, and the directional hypothesis would be retained.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Difference-in-differences — young birth cohorts (exposed to INPRES schools) compared to older cohorts (not exposed), in high-intensity districts compared to low-intensity districts; the interaction of program intensity × cohort exposure identifies the causal effect

key_variables.treatment: INPRES program intensity (number of new schools built per 1,000 children in the district of birth) × cohort exposure (born 1968-1972, young enough to benefit)
key_variables.control: older birth cohorts (born 1950-1962, too old to benefit from new primary schools) in the same districts
key_variables.outcome: years of education; log monthly wages; labor force participation
key_variables.time_period: Program: 1973-1978; Outcomes measured in 1995 survey; Birth cohorts: 1950-1972

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The INPRES school construction program significantly increased educational attainment and adult wages for exposed cohorts. Each school built per 1,000 children increased average education by 0.12-0.19 years and increased wages by 1.5-2.7% for the exposed cohorts relative to older cohorts in the same district.
_ground_truth.main_effect: One additional school per 1,000 children increased education by 0.12-0.19 years and wages by 1.5-2.7% for exposed cohorts; the implied return to education (IV/Wald estimate) is approximately 6.8-10.6%
key_robustness: Controlling for district characteristics interacted with cohort dummies
Alternative definitions of exposed vs. control cohorts
Falsification test: program intensity should not predict outcomes for older (control) cohorts
Regional sub-sample analysis (Java vs. outer islands)
Using birth region (rather than current region) to avoid migration bias

identification_strategy_detail.method: DID: program intensity (continuous, schools per 1,000 children in birth district) interacted with cohort exposure (young enough to benefit from new schools)
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Number of INPRES schools constructed per 1,000 children in district of birth (continuous intensity measure) × binary indicator for exposed birth cohort (born 1968-1972)
identification_strategy_detail.event_window: Program implemented 1973-1978; treated cohorts aged 2-6 at start
identification_strategy_detail.unit_of_observation: Individual male from 1995 SUPAS, identified by birth district and birth year
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Parallel trends: absent the school construction program, education and wage trends for young cohorts would have been the same in high-intensity and low-intensity districts. Supported by: (a) allocation was based on pre-program enrollment (rule-based, not endogenous to future trends); (b) placebo tests on older cohorts show no differential trends.

key_magnitudes.education_effect: 0.12-0.19 additional years of education per school built per 1,000 children (for exposed cohorts)
key_magnitudes.wage_effect: 1.5-2.7% higher wages per school per 1,000 children (for exposed cohorts)
key_magnitudes.implied_return: 6.8-10.6% return to an additional year of education (Wald/IV estimate: wage effect / education effect)

_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: Falsification tests confirm that program intensity does not predict education or wages for older cohorts (born before 1962). Results are robust to including district-level controls interacted with cohort dummies (pre-program enrollment, population density, district-level expenditure). The allocation rule (more schools in low-enrollment districts) creates variation that is driven by policy rather than local demand shocks.
